# Learn business context

## Goal
Understand the website and the person behind it well enough to make useful content recommendations. Approach this like a freelancer getting to know a new client: do your homework, form an initial picture, and improve it through conversation.

The site might represent a business, an artist, a community or a hobby. Adapt what you investigate and ask to its purpose rather than forcing every owner into a business framework.

## Suggested approach

### Start with what is already known
Look through the conversation and existing notes. Identify the website from that information; if needed, ask for the website and a little essential context together. For an ongoing relationship, build on what you have already learned rather than starting the interview again.

Work in batches that respect the user's time. Explain what you will research and what they can expect next, then complete a useful research pass before returning with your initial picture and a short batch of related questions. Avoid repeatedly asking one question, spending several minutes researching, and coming back for another. This is an asynchronous-friendly conversation, not a promise of background execution.

### Research the public picture
Explore the website and relevant public information. The homepage, about page, products or services, published work, articles, reviews and social presence can reveal what the owner does, whom they reach and how they present themselves.

Do enough light market and competitor research to understand the surrounding landscape. Consider not only similar businesses or sites, but other ways the audience meets the same need. This is orientation, not an exhaustive competitive study.

Build an initial interpretation of the site's purpose, audience, offer or subject matter, positioning and voice. Keep useful links and notes so important conclusions can be revisited. Be clear where you are interpreting rather than repeating something the owner has confirmed.

### Invite additional context
Ask whether the user has useful material in Notion, Google Drive or elsewhere that they would like to connect or share. Examples include research, company information, customer conversations, strategy notes or previous content plans. If they do, use it to deepen or challenge the public picture. Public research can still be useful without private documents.

### Discuss and refine your understanding
Share a concise view of what you think you have learned, then group the questions that would most improve the next piece of work into a small, answerable batch. Include the invitation to share private material when it fits, rather than creating another interruption just for that. Explain what their answers will help you do next. Keep this conversational, not a long questionnaire or a step-by-step interview.

Let the user's answers change your interpretation and guide further investigation. We do not need a complete understanding on day one: address what matters now and learn the rest through ongoing work.

Useful areas to explore may include:
- What the business or website exists to do, and what success looks like to its owner.
- Who it serves, what those people want, and how they describe their needs.
- Its products, services or subject matter, and its business model where relevant.
- The alternatives its audience considers and what makes this site worth choosing or returning to.
- Questions, objections or misunderstandings the content should address.
- Experience, examples or other proof the owner can contribute.
- The voice they want and what they hope a visitor will do next.

Choose the areas that matter to this project. An artist may care about commissions or showing their work; a hobby site may care about sharing knowledge or building a community. Do not invent commercial goals where there are none.

### Keep the understanding useful
Save what you learn in the existing business or website knowledge notes, updating them as the conversation develops. Integrate the owner's corrections instead of leaving them in chat. If a useful question remains, ask it; if it can wait, explain the uncertainty without letting it prevent unrelated progress.

Use judgment about how much detail the current task needs. The aim is a working understanding that improves the next piece of work, not a profile completed for its own sake.

## Tools and integrations
Prefer available search and webpage-reading services, such as Composio web search and Context.dev, or another suitable search/scraping API or MCP tool. If a capability is missing and integration discovery or configuration tools are available, use them to find and, where authorized, enable an appropriate integration. Reuse ready project connections before asking the user to create an account. Request connection setup only when it is actually needed, and verify that the tool works for the task. Do not assume every catalog integration is already usable. Use browser or direct HTTP access when no suitable integration is available or it cannot provide what the research needs.

For private material, ask what the user has and help them connect or share the relevant source. Check existing access before asking them to set anything up.

## Useful output
A clear, evolving picture of the website, its audience and the owner's goals that later research and writing can use. Present the important insights and useful questions to the owner; keep supporting notes in the knowledge records. Choose the depth and format for the task rather than imposing a fixed profile template.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Keep inputs and learned context connected without mixing them together. Inputs include the website URL, owner answers, shared document links and public research captures. Preserve their origin and date so an important conclusion can be revisited.

Update the existing Knowledge notes with the current understanding, linking back to those inputs and briefly noting meaningful corrections. Keep unanswered questions with the relevant topic, distinguishing what affects current work from what can wait. Later skills should read these notes rather than reconstructing the business from chat.

Use the workspace's existing record identities and metadata rather than creating a second profile database. Existing production context in agent-files/00-context remains authoritative; public research and raw captures belong under agent-files/01-research with links from the context. For app-owned work, use the corresponding input, Knowledge and Discovery records under the editorial-workspace procedure. In the current app, source notes live in agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/inputs/, learned context in knowledge/, and research syntheses in discoveries/. Link them instead of duplicating the same editable profile. Reuse existing production context files in agent-files/00-context/; keep research in dated agent-files/01-research/ folders with raw/ beside each synthesis. Update agent-files/INDEX.md for durable additions. Any recovery copy of an app-owned result is labeled an archive. Exact field schemas can be refined during wiring; these input/output locations apply now.
